## Overview

This page documents the configuration systems for both the PyTorch and TurboMind inference engines in LMDeploy. Engine configuration controls all aspects of model inference including performance parameters, memory management, parallelism strategies, and optimization settings.

**Scope**: This page covers the configuration data structures and parameters defined in `lmdeploy/messages.py` and `lmdeploy/pytorch/config.py`. For implementation details of the engines themselves, see [TurboMind Engine](2.1) and [PyTorch Engine](2.2).

## Configuration Architecture

Engine configurations follow a hierarchical structure where a top-level engine config (`PytorchEngineConfig` or `TurbomindEngineConfig`) is decomposed into specialized sub-configurations during engine initialization.

### Configuration Flow Diagram

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "User Layer"
        "UserPyTorch" -->|"PytorchEngineConfig\nlmdeploy.messages"| "ConfigBuilder"
        "UserTurboMind" -->|"TurbomindEngineConfig\nlmdeploy.messages"| "TM_Update"
    end

    subgraph "PyTorch Engine Initialization"
        "ConfigBuilder" -->|"lmdeploy.pytorch.engine.config_builder"| "SchedulerConfig"
        "ConfigBuilder" --> "CacheConfig"
        "ConfigBuilder" --> "BackendConfig"
        "ConfigBuilder" --> "DistConfig"

        "SchedulerConfig" -->|"max_batches, max_session_len,\neviction_type, prefill_interval"| "PyTorchEngine"
        "CacheConfig" -->|"block_size, num_gpu_blocks,\nnum_cpu_blocks, window_size"| "PyTorchEngine"
        "BackendConfig" -->|"eager_mode, device_type"| "PyTorchEngine"
        "DistConfig" -->|"tp, dp, ep, world_size,\nattn_tp, mlp_tp, moe_tp"| "PyTorchEngine"
    end

    subgraph "TurboMind Model Initialization"
        "TM_Update" -->|"update_parallel_config\nlmdeploy.turbomind.turbomind"| "TM_Model"
        "TM_Model" -->|"TurboMind\nlmdeploy.turbomind.turbomind.TurboMind"| "TurboMindEngine"
    end

    subgraph "Engine Instances"
        "PyTorchEngine" -->|"Engine (PyTorch)\nlmdeploy.pytorch.engine.engine.Engine"| "Runtime"
        "TurboMindEngine" -->|"TurboMind (C++)\n_turbomind.so"| "Runtime"
    end
```

**Sources**: [lmdeploy/pytorch/config.py:88-164](), [lmdeploy/turbomind/turbomind.py:83-110](), [lmdeploy/messages.py:388-580]()

---

## PyTorch Engine Configuration

The PyTorch engine uses the `PytorchEngineConfig` class (defined in `lmdeploy/messages.py`) as the top-level configuration holding all parameters to control engine behavior. During initialization, `ConfigBuilder` in `lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/config_builder.py` parses and transforms this config into internal specialized config objects used by the engine.

### PytorchEngineConfig Parameters Overview

Parameters in `PytorchEngineConfig` can be categorized by their functional role:

| Category      | Parameters                                         | Description                                              |
|---------------|--------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| **Parallelism** | `tp`, `dp`, `ep`, `attn_tp`, `mlp_tp`, `moe_tp` | Pipeline and parallelism degrees (tensor/data/expert)    |
| **Memory & Cache** | `cache_max_entry_count`, `cache_block_seq_len`, `block_size`, `num_gpu_blocks`, `num_cpu_blocks`, `enable_prefix_caching` | Key-value cache sizing and behavior                       |
| **Performance**  | `prefill_interval`, `eager_mode`, `cudagraph_capture_batch_sizes` | Scheduling and CUDA graph capture parameters             |
| **Hardware**     | `device_type`, `distributed_executor_backend` | Device targeting, backend selection                       |
| **Model Handling** | `dtype`, `download_dir`, `revision`, `adapters` | Weight precision, model source, and LoRA adapters        |
| **Disaggregation (PD)** | `role`, `migration_backend` | Role and backend for KV cache migration in disaggregated serving |

### Internal Configuration Classes

#### SchedulerConfig

Controls request scheduling behavior such as max batches processed concurrently, session token limits, eviction policies, and limits on active LoRA adapters.

```python
@dataclass
class SchedulerConfig:
    max_batches: int              # Max concurrent sequences supported
    max_session_len: int          # Max tokens per session (sequence length)
    max_request_output_len: int = 512  # Default output max tokens
    eviction_type: str = 'recompute'   # Eviction strategy for cache
    prefill_interval: int = 16         # Granularity of prefill schedules in tokens
    max_active_adapters: int = 64      # Max number of LoRA adapters simultaneously active
```

#### CacheConfig

Manages KV cache configuration, including block sizes, number of memory blocks on CPU/GPU, caching behavior and quantization policies, prefix caching, and disaggregation roles.

```python
@dataclass
class CacheConfig:
    max_batches: int
    block_size: int                 # Physical tokens per cache block
    num_cpu_blocks: int             # Number of CPU memory cache blocks
    num_gpu_blocks: int             # Number of GPU memory cache blocks
    kernel_block_size: int = -1     # Specialized kernel block size for CUDA kernels
    dcp: int = 1                   # Data parallelism for cache blocks
    window_size: int = -1          # Sliding window size for cache eviction
    cache_max_entry_count: float = 0.8
    max_prefill_token_num: int = 8192
    cudagraph_capture_batch_sizes: list[int] | None = None # Batch sizes for CUDA graph capture
    enable_prefix_caching: bool = False                    # Enable automatic prefix cache reuse
    quant_policy: QuantPolicy = QuantPolicy.NONE           # KV cache quantization policy
    device_type: str = 'cuda'                              # Device type
    num_state_caches: int = None                           # Number of state cache instances
    role: EngineRole = EngineRole.HYBRID                   # Prefill/Decode/Hybrid role for disaggregation
    prefix_cache_state_budget: int | None = None           # Memory budget for prefix cache states
    prefix_cache_decode_state_interval: int = 0            # Interval for prefix cache decode state
    migration_backend: MigrationBackend = MigrationBackend.NONE
    kv_transfer_config: KVTransferConfig = KVTransferConfig()
```

#### DistConfig

Encapsulates distributed execution parameters, including data, tensor and expert parallelism degrees, with ability for distinct TP sizing per Transformer block components.

```python
@dataclass
class DistConfig:
    dp: int
    tp: int
    ep: int
    attn_tp: int
    mlp_tp: int
    moe_tp: int
    mlp_tp_mode: TPMode = TPMode.DEFAULT
```

Many of these detailed parameters and classes are instantiated and configured by `ConfigBuilder`'s static methods based on user-provided `PytorchEngineConfig` fields during the PyTorch engine bootstrap process.

**Sources**: [lmdeploy/pytorch/config.py:96-171](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/config_builder.py:6-157](), [lmdeploy/messages.py:400-570]()

---

## TurboMind Engine Configuration

The TurboMind engine uses the `TurbomindEngineConfig` dataclass from `lmdeploy/messages.py`, which contains the parameters and parallelism settings for the TurboMind C++/CUDA engine.

### Parallelism Configuration Logic

TurboMind’s parallelism configuration is handled mainly in `update_parallel_config(cfg: TurbomindEngineConfig)` in `lmdeploy/turbomind/turbomind.py`. It computes and adjusts degrees of:

- Data Parallelism (DP),
- Tensor Parallelism (TP) for both attention and MLP layers,
- Communication Parallelism (CP),
- Outer Data Parallelism (outer_dp_size).

The product of these values matches device count to efficiently utilize compute resources and minimize communication overhead.

Key points of the logic:

- If DP/TP/CP sizing is preset, it normalizes and completes missing fields.
- It computes the greatest common divisor (GCD) of MLP and Attention DP sizes and adjusts outer DP accordingly.
- The product `attn_dp_size * attn_tp_size * attn_cp_size * outer_dp_size` equals `device_num`.
- The MLP parallel sizes respect `mlp_dp_size` and `mlp_tp_size` relationships with attention sizes to optimize communication.

This logic enables the TurboMind engine to efficiently parallelize inference across multiple GPUs and nodes.

### Key TurboMindEngineConfig Parameters

| Parameter               | Type    | Description                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|---------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `max_batch_size`        | int     | Maximum batch size for inference                                                                    |
| `device_num`            | int     | Number of devices (GPUs) used                                                                       |
| `dp`, `tp`, `ep`, `cp` | int     | Data, tensor, expert and communication parallelism sizes                                            |
| `devices`               | list    | Device IDs used                                                                                      |
| `communicator`          | str     | Communication backend (e.g., 'nccl', 'cuda-ipc', 'native')                                         |
| `moe_a2a_backend`       | str     | Backend for MoE all-to-all communication ('auto', 'deepep', 'default')                              |
| `model_format`          | str     | Model weight format (e.g., 'hf', 'awq', 'gptq', 'fp8', 'mxfp4')                                    |
| `rope_scaling_factor`   | float   | RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) scaling factor                                                    |
| `cache_max_entry_count` | float   | Ratio controlling GPU memory usage for KV cache                                                    |
| `cache_block_seq_len`   | int     | Sequence length for each KV cache block (default 64)                                              |
| `quant_policy`          | int     | KV cache quantization type (similar to PyTorch's `QuantPolicy`)                                   |
| `nnodes`                | int     | Number of nodes for distributed inference                                                          |
| `node_rank`             | int     | Rank of current node within distributed nodes                                                      |
| `max_active_adapters`   | int     | Maximum active LoRA adapters                                                                        |
| `download_dir`          | str     | Directory for model downloads                                                                       |
| `revision`              | str     | Model revision/version                                                                              |

This config controls all aspects of TurboMind engine initialization from device assignment, parallelism, communication setup, to model format and memory management for KV cache.

**Sources**: [lmdeploy/messages.py:510-580](), [lmdeploy/turbomind/turbomind.py:62-104]()

---

## Generation and Sampling Configuration

At runtime, individual request generation behavior is controlled by the `GenerationConfig` dataclass (`lmdeploy/messages.py`). This structure defines parameters for sampling, output constraints, repetition control, and output formatting.

### Notable Parameters in GenerationConfig

| Parameter               | Type        | Default     | Description                                            |
|-------------------------|-------------|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `n`                     | int         | 1           | Number of completion choices generated (only 1 supported currently) |
| `max_new_tokens`        | int         | 512         | Tokens the engine will generate                        |
| `do_sample`             | bool        | False       | Whether to use sampling or greedy decoding             |
| `top_p`                 | float       | 1.0         | Nucleus sampling threshold                             |
| `top_k`                 | int         | None        | Top-k sampling restriction                             |
| `temperature`           | float       | 0.8         | Sampling temperature                                   |
| `repetition_penalty`    | float       | 1.0         | Controls penalty on repeated tokens                    |
| `stop_token_ids`        | list[int]   | None        | Tokens that stop generation when produced             |
| `bad_token_ids`         | list[int]   | None        | Tokens the engine will never generate                  |
| `min_new_tokens`        | int         | None        | Minimum tokens to generate despite stop conditions    |
| `response_format`       | dict        | None        | Instructions for structured response (JSON, Regex, grammar) |
| `with_cache`            | bool        | False       | For disaggregated cache handling                       |
| `repetition_ngram_size` | int         | 0           | N-gram size for early stop on repetition              |

`GenerationConfig` can specify complex constraints on output format using JSON schemas or regular expressions and controls advanced features such as speculative decoding or disaggregation behavior flags.

**Sources**: [lmdeploy/messages.py:70-164]()

---

## API and CLI Integration

The engine configurations are primarily exposed via the LMDeploy CLI (`lmdeploy/cli/serve.py` and `lmdeploy/cli/utils.py`) and consumed by serving code (e.g. `lmdeploy.serve.openai.api_server.py`).

### CLI to Engine Configuration Mapping

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "CLI Parsing"
        CLI_Serve["lmdeploy serve api_server\n(lmdeploy/cli/serve.py)"]
        ArgHelper["ArgumentHelper & utils\n(lmdeploy/cli/utils.py)"]

        CLI_Serve --> ArgHelper
    end

    subgraph "Logic"
        ArgHelper --> ConvertArgs["convert_args()"]
        ArgHelper --> GetSpec["get_speculative_config()"]
        ConvertArgs --> PytorchConfig["PytorchEngineConfig (lmdeploy.messages)"]
        ConvertArgs --> TurboMindConfig["TurbomindEngineConfig (lmdeploy.messages)"]
        GetSpec --> SpecConfig["SpeculativeConfig (lmdeploy.messages)"]
    end

    subgraph "Engine Instantiation"
        PytorchConfig --> PyTorchEngine["PyTorch Engine"]
        TurboMindConfig --> TurboMindEngine["TurboMind Engine"]
        SpecConfig --> Engine["Connected to Engine Instances"]
    end
```

The CLI argument parser supports command-line flags that directly map to these configuration classes, enabling flexible tuning of engines and distributed operation modes. For example:

- `--role` sets the PD disaggregation role (Prefill, Decode, Hybrid).
- `--migration-backend` selects the protocol for KV cache migration.
- `--tp`, `--dp`, `--ep` control parallelism degrees.
- `--cache-max-entry-count` and `--cudagraph-capture-batch-sizes` configure memory and CUDA optimization parameters.

The serving layer then consumes these configuration objects to initialize the corresponding inference engines.

### Notable CLI Arguments for Engine Config

| CLI Argument               | Config Field          | Description                                      |
|----------------------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `--role`                   | `role` (EngineRole)   | Defines node role in disaggregated serving       |
| `--migration-backend`      | `migration_backend`   | KV cache migration protocol                       |
| `--tp`                    | `tp`                  | Tensor parallelism degree                         |
| `--dp`                    | `dp`                  | Data parallelism degree                           |
| `--ep`                    | `ep`                  | Expert parallelism degree                         |
| `--cache-max-entry-count` | `cache_max_entry_count`| Fraction of GPU memory used for KV cache          |
| `--cudagraph-capture-batch-sizes` | `cudagraph_capture_batch_sizes` | Batch sizes to capture CUDA graphs for optimal performance |

**Sources**: [lmdeploy/cli/utils.py:31-35,91-102](), [lmdeploy/cli/serve.py:97-147]()

# Request Management and Session Handling

<details>

## Overview

LMDeploy's request management operates across two levels:

1. **Serving Layer (`AsyncEngine`)**: This orchestrates end-to-end inference request lifecycle from API down to the inference engine. It maintains session states, manages concurrency via handle pooling, coordinates tokenization, multimodal input processing, and interfaces with the backend engine. It is the core engine for the OpenAI-compatible API server and the Python pipeline [[lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py:93-154]]().

2. **Engine Layer (`Engine` + `RequestManager`)**: This controls request routing to the actual model instances, manages the request queue with prioritization, and executes engine-specific scheduling and inference calls. It handles requests like session addition, token generation, stopping, and ending [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/engine.py:92-185]](), [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:175-387]]().

**Key classes and components:**
- `AsyncEngine`: Main serving interface managing sessions, tokenization, and inference request submission to the engine backend [[lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py:93-154]]().
- `RequestManager`: Internal dispatcher for requests queued to the engine, handling concurrency and callbacks [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:175-432]]().
- `RequestSender`: An interface for engine instances to submit requests to `RequestManager` and await responses [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:67-174]]().
- `SessionManager` and `Session`: Manage conversational state and track requests per session [[lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:17-112]]().
- `RequestHandlePool`: Pools engine handles for concurrency control, ensuring resource reuse [[lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:145-165]]().
- Multi-process Engine Wrappers (`MPEngine`, `RayMPEngine`, `ZMQMPEngine`): Provide abstractions for distributed or multi-process engine execution [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/base.py:28-147]](), [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/ray_engine.py:18-141]](), [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/zmq_engine.py:1-594]]().

---

## System Architecture

### Request Flow and Entity Mapping

The request flow proceeds from a user API call through session management, handle pool acquisition, instance invocation, and finally to low-level request dispatching by `RequestManager`.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Serving_Layer_[Natural_Language_Space]
        AsyncEngine["AsyncEngine<br/>(lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py)"]
        Session["Session<br/>(lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py)"]
        HandlePool["RequestHandlePool<br/>(lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py)"]
    end
    
    subgraph Engine_Layer_[Code_Entity_Space]
        Engine["class Engine<br/>(lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/engine.py)"]
        EngineInstance["class EngineInstance<br/>(lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/engine_instance.py)"]
        RequestManager["class RequestManager<br/>(lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py)"]
        RequestSender["class RequestSender<br/>(lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py)"]
    end
    
    subgraph Request_Definitions
        RequestTypes["enum RequestType:<br/>ADD_SESSION<br/>ADD_MESSAGE<br/>STOP_SESSION<br/>END_SESSION"]
    end
    
    AsyncEngine --> Session
    Session --> HandlePool
    HandlePool --> EngineInstance
    EngineInstance --> RequestSender
    RequestSender --> RequestManager
    Engine --> RequestManager
    RequestManager --> RequestTypes
```

This design cleanly separates user-level session and concurrency concerns from engine-level parallelism and request scheduling.

**Sources**:  
[lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py:93-154](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/engine.py:92-185](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:15-24,67-174,175-431](), [lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:17-35,143-165]()

---

## Core Components

### AsyncEngine (Serving Layer)

The class `AsyncEngine` is the primary entry for user requests and manages the entire lifecycle from input preprocessing to dispatching inference calls and returning responses.

**Key aspects:**

- **Initialization**:
  - Determines sub-backend (`turbomind` or `pytorch`) and loads the corresponding engine instance internally [[lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py:122-154]]().
  - Initializes tokenizer and chat template for prompt construction and processing.
  - Sets the maximum session length and generation configurations.

- **Multimodal Processing**:
  - Uses `MultimodalProcessor` to handle media inputs (images, videos, audio) alongside text [[lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py:135-142]]().

- **Inference & Streaming Generation**:
  - Processes prompts into token IDs.
  - Sends requests asynchronously to backend engine via engine instance handles.
  - Yields token-by-token or chunk-by-chunk results back to caller asynchronously [[lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py:175-225]]().

- **Output Packaging**:
  - Wraps raw backend outputs into `GenOut` dataclass holding tokens, logits, finish reasons.
  - Converts `GenOut` into `Response` objects suitable for API response [[lmdeploy/serve/core/async_engine.py:44-78]]().

### RequestManager and RequestSender (Engine Layer)

- `RequestManager` is responsible for queuing, prioritizing, dispatching, and responding to all engine-level requests like session creation, message adding, stopping, and ending.

- Supports priority ordering for request types for graceful shutdown and quick interruption [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:175-432]]().

- Each engine instance interacts with `RequestManager` indirectly through a `RequestSender` proxy, which manages request IDs, event flags, and response awaiting [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:67-174]]().

**Request/Response Flow:**

```mermaid
graph LR
    Sender["RequestSender<br/>(request.py)"] -->|"send_async()"| ReqQueue["asyncio.Queue<br/>(RequestManager.requests)"]
    ReqQueue --> MainLoop["Engine._loop()"]
    MainLoop --> Handler["Engine._on_add_session<br/>Engine._on_add_message"]
    Handler --> Response["Response<br/>(request.py)"]
    Response -->|"req_manager.response()"| Client["EngineInstance"]
```

**Common Request Types:**

| RequestType    | Function Example           | Description                                            |
| -------------- | --------------------------| ------------------------------------------------------|
| ADD_SESSION    | `async_try_add_session` [[engine_instance.py:32-40]]() | Initializes a new chat session, establishing engine state. |
| STOP_SESSION   | `async_cancel` [[engine_instance.py:43-47]]()         | Interrupts ongoing generation for a session.          |
| END_SESSION    | `end` [[engine_instance.py:61-64]]()                   | Releases session resources and KV cache.               |
| ADD_MESSAGE    | `async_stream_infer` [[engine_instance.py:175-186]]() | Sends tokens for model inference and streaming output. |

**Sources**:  
[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:175-431](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/engine_instance.py:32-64,175-186]()

### Session Management and Request Handle Pooling

High concurrency scenarios are managed by carefully pooling engine instance handles and managing session state independently.

- `Session`: Holds user conversation context, generation configurations, history, and tracks active inference handles per session [[lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:17-110]]().

- `RequestHandlePool`: A fixed-size asyncio.Queue-based pool of engine handles obtained from the `EngineInstance` class. Limits concurrent access to resource-intensive engine instances, preventing overload [[lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:145-165]]().

- `Session.request_handle` provides an async context manager that acquires a handle on request start, and safely returns it when inference completes, with cleanup and abort handling [[lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:77-111]]().

**Sources**:  
[lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:17-112, 145-165]()

---

## Request Lifecycle

### From User API to Model Inference

The flow from a user API request through to backend model inference involves several components interacting asynchronously.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant API as "api_server.py"
    participant AE as "AsyncEngine"
    participant S as "Session"
    participant HP as "RequestHandlePool"
    participant EI as "EngineInstance"
    participant RM as "RequestManager"
    
    API->>AE: generate(session_id, prompt)
    AE->>S: request_handle() acquires handle
    S->>HP: get() EngineInstance handle
    HP-->>S: EngineInstance handle returned
    S->>EI: async_stream_infer(tokens)
    EI->>RM: async_send(ADD_MESSAGE)
    RM-->>EI: Response (async stream)
    loop Streaming Generation
        EI-->>S: EngineOutput chunks
        S-->>AE: GenOut instances
        AE-->>API: Stream Response chunks
    end
    S->>HP: release handle (finally block in request_handle)
```

This sequence ensures that requests are processed asynchronously, sessions maintain consistent state, and backend concurrency is managed safely.

**Sources**:  
[lmdeploy/serve/managers/session_manager.py:77-104](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/engine_instance.py:175-182](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/request.py:161-164]()

---

## Distributed and Multi-Process Engine Wrappers

LMDeploy supports distributing inference workloads via multi-process or multi-node mechanisms, abstracted via `MPEngine`.

- **`MPEngine`**: Base class for multi-process engine implementations. Provides stub collective RPC interfaces for forwarding requests across processes [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/base.py:28-147]]().

- **ZMQ-based Engine (`ZMQMPEngine`)**: Implements RPC communication over ZeroMQ sockets. Uses an async ZMQ server to route engine requests across processes. It monitors process liveness and ensures proper failure semantics [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/zmq_engine.py:1-594]]().

- **Ray-based Engine (`RayMPEngine`)**: Uses Ray actors to distribute engine workers, handle scheduling, and collect streaming results. Supports creating streaming tasks and managing actor lifecycles [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/ray_engine.py:18-141]]().

- **Mailbox System (`StreamMailbox`)**: Provides thread-safe single-slot coalescing mailbox for streaming outputs from remote processes, enabling asynchronous stream handling with buffer/flush semantics [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/base_worker.py:55-62]]().

- **Backend Liveness Tracking (`_RPCServerLiveness`)**: Monitors remote engine process health. When backend crashes, it triggers callbacks to cleanup state and fails pending RPC requests to avoid hangs [[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/zmq_rpc.py:23-45]]().

These multi-process wrappers allow LMDeploy to scale model serving across devices or distributed environments transparently to the session/request flow layers.

**Sources**:  
[lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/base.py:28-147](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/zmq_engine.py:1-257](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/ray_engine.py:18-141](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/base_worker.py:55-62](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/mp_engine/zmq_rpc.py:23-45]()

---

# Summary

LMDeploy's request management and session handling is architected to cleanly separate user-facing conversational state, concurrency management, and low-level engine scheduling. The serving layer (`AsyncEngine`) interfaces with session and handle pools to provide smooth asynchronous request handling, while the engine layer (`Engine` with `RequestManager`) manages request dispatch and prioritization efficiently. Multi-process and distributed serving is abstracted with engine wrappers utilizing ZeroMQ and Ray for scalable deployments. This layered design enables robust, high-throughput, and maintainable LLM serving infrastructure.

## Purpose and Scope

This page documents the detailed implementation of memory management and the blocked KV (Key-Value) cache system within LMDeploy. The KV cache is essential for efficient autoregressive transformer model inference, enabling reuse of previously computed attention keys and values to reduce redundant computation.

Key areas covered include:

- Memory management design with logical and physical block abstraction.
- Block managers and allocation strategies for CPU/GPU blocks including sliding window support.
- Blocked KV cache implementation with prefix caching mechanisms via a block trie.
- Scheduler coordination of sequence lifecycle and KV admission.
- Cache configuration parameters and eviction policies.
- KV cache connectors facilitating external cache sharing and disaggregated serving.

LMDeploy employs a sophisticated blocked cache structure integrated deeply into its PyTorch inference engine, enabling advanced features like cache swapping, prefix sharing, partial recomputation, and distributed KV cache migration.

---

## KV Cache Architecture and Block Management

### Blocked KV Cache Design

LMDeploy's KV cache organizes stored KV tensors as fixed-size **logical blocks**, allowing fine-grained sharing and reuse between sequences. Each sequence maintains a sequence of logical block IDs mapping to physical memory blocks.

- A **BlockManager** oversees allocation and freeing of physical memory blocks split between GPU and CPU.
- Logical blocks translate to physical blocks via `phy_map`.
- Blocks can be swapped between GPU and CPU memory to manage scarce GPU cache capacity.
- Prefix caching shares common prefix blocks across sequences using reference counting and a block trie.
- The block size (tokens per block) is fixed and configurable via `CacheConfig.block_size`.

This structure allows dynamic resource management, evictions, and recomputations on a per-block granularity rather than entire sequences.

#### Logical and Physical Blocks Visualization

```mermaid
graph TB
  subgraph "Logical Blocks (per sequence)"
    SeqA_Block1["LA1"]
    SeqA_Block2["LA2"]
    SeqA_Block3["LA3"]
    SeqB_Block1["LB1"]
    SeqB_Block2["LB2"]
  end

  subgraph "Physical Memory Managed by BlockManager"
    GPU_Block1["P1 (GPU)"]
    GPU_Block2["P2 (GPU)"]
    GPU_Block3["P3 (GPU)"]
    GPU_Block4["P4 (GPU)"]
    CPU_Block1["PC1 (CPU)"]
    CPU_Block2["PC2 (CPU)"]
  end

  SeqA_Block1 -.->|Shared prefix| GPU_Block1
  SeqA_Block2 --> GPU_Block2
  SeqA_Block3 --> GPU_Block3

  SeqB_Block1 -.->|Shared prefix| GPU_Block1
  SeqB_Block2 --> GPU_Block4

  GPU_Block3 -.->|Swapped out| CPU_Block1
```

**Diagram:** Logical-to-Physical mapping of blocked KV cache with GPU/CPU memory and shared prefix blocks.

Sources:  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/scheduler.py:1-160]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/block_manager/default_block_manager.py:1-153]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/block_manager/window_block_manager.py:1-109]()

---

### Block Managers

LMDeploy provides multiple block manager implementations controlling block allocations and eviction policies.

**DefaultBlockManager**: Allocates physical blocks on demand; free block pool tracked with logical-to-physical map. Supports GPU and CPU pools with reference counting and access time tracking.

- Key methods:
  - `num_required_blocks(sequence, prealloc_size=0)`: Calculate additional blocks needed.
  - `allocate_msg(sequence, prealloc_size=0)`: Allocate logical blocks and map to physical.
  - `free(sequence)`: Frees all blocks belonging to the sequence.
  - Swap methods `try_swap_out`/`try_swap_in` move blocks between devices based on availability.

**WindowBlockManager**: Extends DefaultBlockManager with sliding window support. It drops old prefix blocks from sequences exceeding window size, reclaiming resources proactively to keep working set size bounded.

- Overrides:  
  - `num_required_blocks` to adjust count subtracting dropped blocks.  
  - `can_allocate` to consider droppable blocks as available resources.  
  - `allocate_msg` reuses freed blocks before allocating new ones.

Sources:  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/block_manager/default_block_manager.py:17-153]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/block_manager/window_block_manager.py:24-109]()

---

## Scheduler and Sequence Lifecycle

### Scheduler Class Overview

The `Scheduler` class coordinates sequence lifecycles, memory admission, and caching metadata.

- **Sessions and Sequences**: Scheduler holds sessions containing sequences, managing their states (WAITING, READY, RUNNING, STOPPED).
- **Block and State Managers**: Uses `block_manager` to handle KV cache blocks and `state_manager` for runtime states (SSM layers).
- **BlockTrie**: Implements prefix caching, mapping token block sequences to saved cache checkpoints for reusing cached prefixes.
- **EvictionHelper**: Implements eviction policies (e.g., recompute) to free blocks when capacity is constrained.
- **KV Connectors**: Interfaces to external KV state sharing or remote cache protocols.
- **Admission Control and Prefill Scheduler**: Handles scheduling order and distills which sequences can run based on resource availability.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Scheduler {
        +schedule()
        +add_session(session_id)
        +end_session(session_id)
        -tick()
    }
    class Session {
        +add_sequence(token_ids)
        +sequences
    }
    class SequenceLifecycle {
        +add_sequence(seq, status)
        +remove_sequence(seq)
        +end_sequence(seq)
        +release_paging_resources(seq)
    }
    class BlockManager
    class StateManager
    class BlockTrie
    class EvictionHelper
    class KVLoadCoordinator
    class KVSaveCoordinator

    Scheduler --> Session : manages >
    Scheduler --> SequenceLifecycle : lifecycle >
    Scheduler --> BlockManager : manages blocks >
    Scheduler --> StateManager : manages states >
    Scheduler --> BlockTrie : prefix caching >
    Scheduler --> EvictionHelper : eviction policy >
    Scheduler --> KVLoadCoordinator : load admission >
    Scheduler --> KVSaveCoordinator : save coordination >
```

**Diagram:** Scheduler class and its associated resource managers and coordinators.

### Sequence States and Transitions

The `SequenceLifecycle` class is responsible for:

- Adding/removing sequences.
- Transitioning between states: WAITING → READY → RUNNING → STOPPED.
- Managing paging resources on state changes.
- Notes sequences with external backing states (SSM models).

States are implemented as subclasses of `StateBase` with methods for `activate()`, `evict()`, and lifecycle transitions.

Sources:  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/scheduler.py:63-160]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/seq_states/states.py:13-189]()

---

## Cache Configuration and Eviction

### CacheConfig Parameters

The main cache configuration parameters influencing memory behavior include:

| Parameter                      | Description                                       |
|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| `block_size`                  | Tokens per logical block stored in KV cache.    |
| `num_gpu_blocks`              | Total GPU blocks available (cache capacity).    |
| `num_cpu_blocks`              | Total CPU blocks assigned for swap space.       |
| `max_batches`                 | Max batch count allowed for inference.          |
| `window_size`                 | Applies for sliding window block manager modes. |
| `enable_prefix_caching`       | Enables prefix sharing via block trie.          |
| `quant_policy`                | The quantization policy to reduce cache memory. |

- `enable_prefix_caching` is automatically disabled when sliding window usage is detected.
- Quantization supported policies include INT4, INT8, FP8, and TurboMind-specific schemes for memory savings.
- Multi-head latent attention (MLA) support requires a special FP8 cache format.

### Eviction Policies

The eviction helper orchestrates freeing cache blocks by:

- Identifying sequences safe to evict or recompute to free up space.
- Eviction triggers when cache cannot allocate new blocks for incoming sequences.
- Uses lazy eviction via block trie prefix evictions to reclaim cache blocks.
- For SSM-enabled models, eviction also manages state checkpoint availability.
  
Sources:  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/eviction_helper/recompute_eviction_helper.py:1-130]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/scheduler.py:131-160]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/block_manager/window_block_manager.py:24-109]()

---

## Prefix Caching via BlockTrie

The prefix caching mechanism allows multiple sequences to share cached KV blocks of identical prefix tokens.

- `BlockTrie` implements a trie where each node corresponds to a contiguous block of tokens (block granularity).
- During prefill, sequences query the trie to match prefixes, reuse physical blocks, and avoid recomputing cached prefixes.
- The `BlockTrie` also manages state checkpoint lifecycle for models with SSM layers.
- When memory is constrained, the trie evicts less recently used blocks to make capacity.

### Data Flow for Prefix Cache Matching

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Scheduler
    participant BlockTrie
    participant BlockManager
    participant SequenceLifecycle

    Scheduler->>BlockTrie: match(sequence prefix blocks)
    alt prefix found
        BlockTrie->>Scheduler: return matched cache blocks
        Scheduler->>BlockManager: pin blocks and maintain refs
        Scheduler->>SequenceLifecycle: transition to READY with cached blocks
    else prefix not found
        Scheduler->>SequenceLifecycle: transition to WAITING for full prefill
    end
```

Sources:  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/scheduler.py:108-160]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/block_trie/trie.py:1-200 (partial inferred)]()  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/block_trie/checkpoint_lifecycle.py:1-150 (partial inferred)]()

---

## KV Connectors for Remote Cache Sharing

KV connectors interface LMDeploy with external KV cache storage, enabling:

- Remote cache loading and saving via `KVLoadCoordinator` and `KVSaveCoordinator`.
- Sharing KV cache across processes or nodes in disaggregated serving.
- Handling asynchronous communication for KV cache migration in speculative decoding or multi-engine setups.

Connectors must implement callbacks for:

- `on_new_request(sequence)`: to track new cached requests.
- `request_finished(sequence)`: to synchronize upon sequence completion.

This modular design enables sophisticated cache migration and sharing policies.

Sources:  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/paging/scheduler.py:63-160]()

---

## Input Construction and Chunking

The `InputsMakerAsync` module converts scheduling decisions into concrete inputs packaged as `ModelInputs` for the model.

- Splits excessive prefill tokens into model-safe chunks via `LongContextChunker`.
- Manages multimodal input spans that cannot be split.
- Generates state cache copy plans for saving/restoring SSM prefix caches.
- Prepares data blobs for the executor, respecting multiprocess ranks and decoding strategies.

Sources:  
- [lmdeploy/pytorch/engine/inputs_maker.py:50-170]()

---

## Summary Diagram: From Natural Language Request to KV Cache Management

```mermaid
graph TD
  subgraph "Natural Language Processing"
    UserRequest["User Request / Prompt"]
    Tokenizer["Tokenizer"]
    TokenizedInput["Tokenized Input Tokens"]
  end

  subgraph "Inference Engine (PyTorch)"
    Scheduler["Scheduler (lmdeploy.pytorch.paging.scheduler.Scheduler)"]
    SequenceLifecycle["SequenceLifecycle (lmdeploy.pytorch.paging.seq_states.states.SequenceLifecycle)"]
    BlockManager["BlockManager (default or window)"]
    StateManager["StateManager"]
    BlockTrie["BlockTrie (Prefix Cache)"]
    EvictionHelper["EvictionHelper (RecomputeEvictionHelper etc.)"]
    KVLoadCoord["KVLoadCoordinator"]
    KVSaveCoord["KVSaveCoordinator"]
    InputsMaker["InputsMakerAsync (lmdeploy.pytorch.engine.inputs_maker.InputsMakerAsync)"]
    ModelAgent["ModelAgent"]
  end

  subgraph "Physical Memory and Storage"
    GPUCache["GPU Memory Blocks"]
    CPUCache["CPU Memory Blocks (Swap)"]
    RemoteCache["External KV Cache (via KV Connectors)"]
  end

  UserRequest --> Tokenizer --> TokenizedInput --> Scheduler
  Scheduler --> SequenceLifecycle
  Scheduler --> BlockManager
  Scheduler --> StateManager
  Scheduler --> BlockTrie
  Scheduler --> EvictionHelper
  Scheduler --> KVLoadCoord
  Scheduler --> KVSaveCoord

  Scheduler --> InputsMaker
  InputsMaker --> ModelAgent

  BlockManager --> GPUCache
  BlockManager --> CPUCache
  KVLoadCoord <---> RemoteCache
  KVSaveCoord <---> RemoteCache
```

**Diagram:** Overview connecting natural language input processing through scheduler and memory management layers to physical KV cache memory and external KV connectors.

---

# Summary

LMDeploy's memory management and blocked KV cache system is designed for flexible, high-performance transformer inference scaling. It leverages fixed-size logical blocks managed by a BlockManager to efficiently map cached KV tensors in GPU and CPU memory.

The Scheduler orchestrates KV cache lifecycle and admission, leveraging prefix caching through a BlockTrie to share computation prefixes and reduce repeated work. Eviction helpers implement policies for freeing memory by recomputation or stopping sequences. KV connectors extend cache sharing beyond local memory for distributed serving.

Together these components deliver a powerful foundation for efficient large language model deployment and advanced features such as speculative decoding, disaggregated serving, and cache quantization.

---

## Overview

Model Management in LMDeploy refers to the comprehensive system responsible for discovering, loading, configuring, and preparing models for efficient inference. It supports a variety of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) from diverse sources, including local directories and popular hubs like HuggingFace.

Core responsibilities of this system include:
- Model architecture detection
- Backend engine selection (TurboMind or PyTorch)
- Chat prompt template application
- Tokenization and detokenization
- Model loading and format conversion
- Optimization tasks such as quantization and tensor parallelism

This page provides a high-level overview of how LMDeploy manages these aspects. For detailed technical information, please refer to the respective child pages:
- Chat Templates and Tokenization: [Chat Templates and Tokenization](#3.1)
- Model Loading and Conversion: [Model Loading and Conversion](#3.2)
- Quantization Techniques: [Quantization Techniques](#3.3)

---

## Model Sources and Discovery

LMDeploy supports models located in:
- Local directories (e.g., converted TurboMind format or local checkpoints)
- Remote HuggingFace or ModelScope repositories

If a model path is non-existent locally, LMDeploy automatically fetches it from the specified hub using utility functions like `get_model()` [lmdeploy/vl/model/builder.py:51-54]().

For tokenizer initialization, LMDeploy relies on HuggingFace’s `AutoTokenizer` for consistent handling, including support for `trust_remote_code` modes that enable custom tokenizer classes [lmdeploy/tokenizer.py:46-50]().

The `get_model_arch()` function serves as the entry point to load the model configuration from the local path or remote hub, returning both the architecture string identifier and pretrained config object that downstream components rely on [lmdeploy/archs.py:135-155]().

**Sources:**  
[lmdeploy/archs.py:135-155](), [lmdeploy/tokenizer.py:46-50](), [lmdeploy/vl/model/builder.py:51-54]()

---

## Architecture Detection System

Identifying the architecture of a model is fundamental to selecting appropriate model handlers, backends, and loading logic. The `get_model_arch()` function implements a tiered strategy:

```mermaid
%% Architecture Detection Flow
graph TB
  MP["model_path (str)"] --> CFG_LOAD["config_from_pretrained(model_path)"]
  CFG_LOAD --> CFG_DICT["cfg.to_dict()"]

  CFG_DICT --> ARCH1["cfg['architectures'][0]"]
  CFG_DICT --> ARCH2["cfg['auto_map']"]
  CFG_DICT --> ARCH3["cfg['language_config']['auto_map']"]

  subgraph ArchExtraction
    ARCH1
    ARCH2
    ARCH3
  end

  ArchExtraction --> ARCH["arch (str), e.g. 'LlamaForCausalLM'"]
  CFG_LOAD --> CFG["cfg (PretrainedConfig)"]

  return_values["Return (arch, cfg)"] --> ARCH
  return_values --> CFG
```

Key notes:
- The function tries to extract the primary model class name from the config's `architectures` field first.
- If not found, it probes `auto_map` and nested `language_config` for autoregressive causal LM classes.
- Results guide later processes in model registry lookup and engine configuration.

LMDeploy also uses `check_vl_llm()` to detect if a model is a Vision-Language Model (VLM) by inspecting config fields like `vision_config` and specific architecture names [lmdeploy/archs.py:84-114]().

**Sources:**  
[lmdeploy/archs.py:135-160](), [lmdeploy/archs.py:84-114]()

---

## Backend Compatibility and Selection

Depending on model architecture and supported features, LMDeploy routes inference to either the **TurboMind** engine (highly optimized C++/CUDA) or the **PyTorch** engine (pure Python with CUDA support). Backend selection is performed by `autoget_backend()`:

```mermaid
%% Backend Selection Logic
graph TB
  MP["model_path"] --> ARCH_GET["get_model_arch(model_path)"]
  MP --> TRITON_CHECK["Check triton_models directory"]

  ARCH_GET --> SUPPORTED["Is arch in TurboMind SUPPORTED_ARCHS?"]
  SUPPORTED -->|Yes| QUANT_CHECK["Check quant_method (e.g. smooth_quant)"]
  QUANT_CHECK -->|smooth_quant| PYTORCH_BACKEND["Use PyTorch Engine"]
  QUANT_CHECK -->|else| WINDOW_ATTN_CHECK["Does model use window attention?"]
  WINDOW_ATTN_CHECK -->|True| PYTORCH_BACKEND
  WINDOW_ATTN_CHECK -->|False| TURBOMIND_BACKEND["Use TurboMind Engine"]

  TRITON_CHECK -->|Exists| TURBOMIND_BACKEND
  TURBOMIND_BACKEND --> AUTOGET["autoget_backend() returns 'turbomind'"]
  PYTORCH_BACKEND --> AUTOGET2["autoget_backend() returns 'pytorch'"]
```

Summary:
- TurboMind supports a wide set of models including Llama (up to 3.2), InternLM, Qwen (up to 3.5), InternVL, and other advanced architectures [lmdeploy/turbomind/supported_models.py:7-76]() and [docs/en/supported_models/supported_models.md:5-53]() .
- If model uses window attention (e.g., Mistral, Qwen1.5 with `use_sliding_window`), TurboMind does not support it, and system falls back to PyTorch.
- Models with quantization methods incompatible with TurboMind (e.g., SmoothQuant) also fall back to PyTorch.
- The presence of a local `triton_models` directory is a direct signal to use TurboMind’s engine.

**Sources:**  
[lmdeploy/archs.py:10-51](), [lmdeploy/turbomind/supported_models.py:7-76](), [docs/en/supported_models/supported_models.md:5-53]()

---

## Model Registry and Mapping

LMDeploy maintains two core registries to map user-facing model identifiers to implementation classes and logic:

### Chat Template Registry (`MODELS`)

The chat template abstraction governs how user inputs are formatted into prompts sent to models.

- `MODELS` is a registry of chat template handlers keyed by model name [lmdeploy/model.py:14]()  
- Templates are defined as dataclasses `ChatTemplateConfig` holding parameters like system prompts, user/assistant prompt delimiters, and model capability (`'chat'`, `'completion'`, etc.) [lmdeploy/model.py:36-70]()  
- `BaseChatTemplate` provides generic prompt concatenation logic [lmdeploy/model.py:114-142]()  
- Many supported models provide specialized templates registered in `MODELS`, including `hf` which wraps HuggingFace's own chat template methods [tests/test_lmdeploy/test_model.py:5-55]()  
- The config supports serializing from and to JSON for ease of editing and reuse [lmdeploy/model.py:83-111]()

This abstraction enables consistent chat interactions tailored individually per model architecture or brand.

### PyTorch Model Module Mapping

For the PyTorch engine, LMDeploy maps HuggingFace architecture class names to internal optimized implementations via the `MODULE_MAP`:

| HuggingFace Architecture                        | LMDeploy PyTorch Implementation Path                                |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `LlamaForCausalLM`                             | `lmdeploy.pytorch.models.llama.LlamaForCausalLM`                  |
| `InternLM2ForCausalLM`                         | `lmdeploy.pytorch.models.internlm2.InternLM2ForCausalLM`          |
| `Qwen3ForCausalLM`                             | `lmdeploy.pytorch.models.qwen3.Qwen3ForCausalLM`                  |
| `DeepseekV3ForCausalLM`                        | `lmdeploy.pytorch.models.deepseek_v2.DeepseekV2ForCausalLM`       |
| `InternVLChatModel`                            | `lmdeploy.pytorch.models.internvl.InternVLChatModel`              |

This modular design allows extending support for new models by registering new classes within `MODULE_MAP` [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/module_map.py:1-273]().

**Sources:**  
[lmdeploy/model.py:14-110](), [tests/test_lmdeploy/test_model.py:5-55](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/module_map.py:1-273]()

---

## Model Configuration Hierarchy

LMDeploy uses layered configuration classes to parameterize model behavior and the inference environment:

| Configuration Class         | Purpose                                   | Key Attributes                                                                                       |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ChatTemplateConfig`       | Parameters for chat prompt formatting     | `model_name`, `system`, `user`, `assistant`, `stop_words` [lmdeploy/model.py:57-70]()              |
| `PytorchEngineConfig`      | PyTorch backend engine settings           | `tp` (tensor parallelism), `session_len`, `block_size`, etc. [lmdeploy/archs.py:4]()               |
| `TurbomindEngineConfig`    | TurboMind backend engine settings         | `tp`, `model_format`, `cache_block_seq_len`, and other tuning parameters [lmdeploy/archs.py:4]()   |

These configs can be auto-generated or customized and passed through in the loading pipeline to finely control model deployment aspects such as parallelism and memory options.

**Sources:**  
[lmdeploy/model.py:57-70](), [lmdeploy/archs.py:4-90]()

---

## Integration with Vision-Language Models (VLMs)

LMDeploy also handles multi-modal models with vision encoders via specialized builders:

- The VL builder function `load_vl_model()` supports loading vision models along with optional LLM backbones, conditional on the backend and configuration [lmdeploy/vl/model/builder.py:37-86]()  
- The system matches HuggingFace configs with registered VLM classes in `VISION_MODELS` and builds preprocessors accordingly  
- TurboMind may run vision encoders natively in C++, while PyTorch runs the full model including vision and language components.

This separation allows efficient multi-modal inference leveraging LMDeploy’s flexible backend framework.

---

## Summary: Model Management Workflow

```mermaid
%% High-Level Model Management Workflow
graph TD
  UserInput["User provides model path or ID"] --> SourceCheck["Check Local Path / Download (get_model)"]

  SourceCheck --> LoadConfig["Load Config & Detect Architecture (get_model_arch)"]

  LoadConfig --> BackendSelect["Select Backend (autoget_backend)"]

  BackendSelect --> |TurboMind| TurboMindLoad["TurboMind Model Loader"]
  BackendSelect --> |PyTorch| PyTorchLoad["PyTorch Model Loader"]

  TurboMindLoad --> ChatTemplateCreate["Instantiate Chat Template (ChatTemplateConfig + MODELS)"]
  PyTorchLoad --> ChatTemplateCreate

  ChatTemplateCreate --> TokenizerInit["Initialize Tokenizer (HuggingFaceTokenizer)"]

  TokenizerInit --> Quantization["Apply Quantization (if enabled)"]

  Quantization --> ReadyForServing["Model ready for inference serving"]
```

This schematic maps the user-facing natural language elements such as "model path" and "chat template" to explicit code entities like `get_model_arch()`, `autoget_backend()`, `ChatTemplateConfig`, and `HuggingFaceTokenizer`.

# Page: Chat Templates and Tokenization

# Chat Templates and Tokenization

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

## Purpose and Scope

This page details LMDeploy's chat template system and tokenization framework, explaining how conversational prompts are structured and tokenized for various large language model (LLM) families. It covers:

- The `ChatTemplateConfig` dataclass for defining chat prompt templates with system, user, assistant, and tool message components.
- The `MODELS` registry which holds registered chat templates keyed by model names.
- The fallback mechanism to HuggingFace (`HFChatTemplate`) for models without pre-defined templates.
- The tokenization and detokenization layer, encapsulated primarily by `HuggingFaceTokenizer`.
- Integration with architecture detection and model loading flow to select appropriate templates and backend.

This mechanism serves as the critical bridge from OpenAI-like multi-message chat inputs to the exact prompt string formats required by backend LLM implementations.

---

## System Overview

### Chat Template System

The chat template system adapts messages into model-specific prompt strings according to each model family's conventions. It supports multiple roles (`system`, `user`, `assistant`, and optional `tool`) and message delimiters configured in `ChatTemplateConfig`. The system manages special tokens, capabilities (`completion`, `chat`, `infilling`, `python`), and stop words.

Templates are generally registered in the global registry `MODELS`. If a requested model's template is missing, LMDeploy falls back to a universal HuggingFace-based template class (`HFChatTemplate`) that invokes the tokenizer's native `apply_chat_template` method to produce the prompt string, preserving compatibility.

### Tokenization and Detokenization

Tokenization wraps the HuggingFace `AutoTokenizer` to provide consistent vocab size reporting, prefix space handling, and incremental detokenization state tracking through `DetokenizeState`. This layer is designed for efficient token-level and partial decoding operations, which is essential in streaming and interactive scenarios.

### Architecture and Backend Integration

The template system ties closely with the architecture detection logic from `archs.py` which selects between TurboMind or PyTorch backends based on model compatibility. Model architectures are also used to identify an appropriate chat template in `MODELS` by name or via the HuggingFace fallback.

---

## Data Flow Diagram: From Input Message to Backend Prompt String

```mermaid
graph TB
    UserInput["OpenAI-style Messages Array"]
    ChatTemplateConfig["ChatTemplateConfig instance\n(lmdeploy/model.py:35)"]
    MODELS["MODELS Registry\n(lmdeploy/model.py:14)"]
    HFChatTemplate["HFChatTemplate Fallback\n(lmdeploy/model.py:678)"]
    PromptString["Formatted Prompt String"]
    Tokenizer["HuggingFaceTokenizer\n(lmdeploy/tokenizer.py:39)"]

    UserInput -->|passed to| ChatTemplateConfig
    ChatTemplateConfig -->|instantiates template class from| MODELS
    MODELS -->|if missing, fallback to| HFChatTemplate
    HFChatTemplate -->|uses| Tokenizer
    MODELS -->|calls messages2prompt()| PromptString
    HFChatTemplate -->|calls tokenizer.apply_chat_template()| PromptString
```

**Sources:** [lmdeploy/model.py:14-111](), [lmdeploy/model.py:678-775](), [lmdeploy/tokenizer.py:39-180]()

---

## ChatTemplateConfig Dataclass

The `ChatTemplateConfig` dataclass encapsulates chat formatting parameters, enabling consistent prompt building.

### Key Fields

| Field             | Type                             | Description                                          | Example                                |
|-------------------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `model_name`      | `str`                           | Unique template identifier, maps to a registered template class. | `'llama2'` or `'internlm'`           |
| `model_path`      | `str | None`                   | Optional model path for HuggingFace templates fallback. | `'model/hf/path'`                    |
| `system`          | `str | None`                   | Start of system message section.                     | `'[INST] <<SYS>>\n'`                  |
| `meta_instruction`| `str | None`                   | System prompt content.                               | `'You are a helpful assistant.'`      |
| `eosys`           | `str | None`                   | End of system prompt section.                        | `'\n<</SYS>>\n\n'`                    |
| `user`            | `str | None`                   | Start of user prompt.                                | `'USER: '`                           |
| `eoh`             | `str | None`                   | End of user prompt.                                  | `' '`                               |
| `assistant`       | `str | None`                   | Start of assistant/AI response prompt.              | `'ASSISTANT: '`                      |
| `eoa`             | `str | None`                   | End of assistant prompt.                             | `'</s>'`                            |
| `tool`            | `str | None`                   | Start of a tool prompt (optional).                   | `''`                               |
| `eotool`          | `str | None`                   | End of tool prompt (optional).                        | `''`                               |
| `separator`       | `str | None`                   | Text separating assistant prompt parts (optional).  | `' '`                              |
| `capability`      | `Literal`                      | Capability type: `'completion'`, `'chat'`, `'infilling'`, `'python'` | `'chat'`                           |
| `stop_words`      | `List[str] | None`             | List of stop words for decoding generation termination. | `['</s>', '<|im_end|>']`          |

### Core Methods

- `chat_template()`  
  Instantiates and returns the registered template class (or `BaseChatTemplate` fallback) according to `model_name`. It passes all other fields as parameters.

- `messages2prompt(messages)`  
  Converts a list of OpenAI-style message dicts (role, content) into a properly structured prompt string by concatenating segments defined by chat template fields, including system, user, assistant, and tool delimiters.

- JSON serialization: `to_json()` and `from_json()` for saving/loading configs.

---

## MODELS Registry and Core Template Classes

The `MODELS` registry is a global mmengine Registry keyed by template name. Key template classes include:

| Template Name    | Class Name         | Supported Models / Description                        | File Location                      |
|------------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| `base`           | `BaseChatTemplate` | Generic default chat template fallback               | [lmdeploy/model.py:113-181]()    |
| `vicuna`         | `Vicuna`           | Vicuna and WizardLM chat models                       | [lmdeploy/model.py:238-270]()    |
| `internlm`       | `InternLMChat7B`   | InternLM 7B - 20B chat models                         | [lmdeploy/model.py:310-338]()    |
| `llama2`          | `Llama2`           | Llama 2 and Code Llama chat and completion templates | [lmdeploy/model.py:373-408]()    |
| `codellama`      | `CodeLlama`        | CodeLlama with support for infilling and python specialist mode | [lmdeploy/model.py:409-464]()    |
| `hf`             | `HFChatTemplate`   | Universal HuggingFace fallback calling library tokenizer | [lmdeploy/model.py:678-775]()    |
| `qwen3`          | `Qwen3`            | Qwen 3.x chat templates                               | [lmdeploy/model.py:896]()  |

### BaseChatTemplate

The base template supports a flexible chat formatting mechanism with customizable delimiters around each message role. It implements:

- `get_prompt(prompt)`: Returns a concatenated prompt for a single user input.
- `messages2prompt(messages)`: Converts multiple messages to prompt by filling delimiters appropriately.
- Handles capability like `completion` (without special formatting).
- Uses role-to-delimiter mappings (`box_map` and `eox_map`) to concatenate messages.

### HFChatTemplate (Universal Fallback)

`HFChatTemplate` wraps HuggingFace tokenizer's own `.apply_chat_template()` method, used for many models that come with native prompt formatting, enabling out-of-the-box use without manual template definitions. It supports:

- Loading tokenizer from `transformers` with `trust_remote_code=True`.
- Tokenizing messages and applying model-predefined chat templates.
- This fallback ensures compatibility with new or custom HuggingFace models.

---

## Specialized Chat Template Capabilities

### CodeLlama Infilling Support

The `CodeLlama` template can handle special infilling tasks using tokens `<PRE>`, `<SUF>`, and `<MID>`:

```python
def _infill_prompt(self, prompt):
    prefix, suffix = prompt.split('<FILL>')
    if self.suffix_first:
        prompt = f'<PRE> <SUF>{suffix} <MID> {prefix}'
    else:
        prompt = f'<PRE> {prefix} <SUF>{suffix} <MID>'
    return prompt
```

It replaces `<FILL>` in the prompt with the infilling markers and swaps suffix/prefix if `suffix_first` is set.

---

## Tokenization and Detokenization Layer

### HuggingFaceTokenizer

- Wraps `transformers.AutoTokenizer` for LMDeploy usage.
- Handles tokenizer version checks against the model configuration.
- Maintains `prefix_space_tokens` to decide when to prepend a space on incremental decoding.
- Implements `indexes_containing_token(token)` to find all vocab indexes containing a specific token string (useful for stop word handling).
- Supports incremental decoding with `DetokenizeState` that stores offsets and previous tokens.

### DetokenizeState

Contains incremental decoding state:

| Field          | Meaning                                                                |
|----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ids_offset`   | Offset applied to token IDs, to handle non-one-to-one output lengths. |
| `prev_tokens`  | Previously decoded tokens (string list).                              |
| `prefix_offset`| Start index of tokens for the current incremental decode.             |
| `read_offset`  | End index of previously read tokens for deduplication.                |

The tokenizer and detokenizer together support streaming outputs and partial decoding in token-granular fashion.

---

## Model Architecture Detection and Chat Template Selection Flow

### Backend and Template Resolution

LMDeploy dynamically chooses the backend (`turbomind` or `pytorch`) via `archs.autoget_backend()` by:

- Inspecting the model path.
- Checking model architecture support in the TurboMind `SUPPORTED_ARCHS` mapping.
- Falling back to PyTorch if TurboMind does not support the model.

Once the backend is selected, the system fetches a chat template from `MODELS` by matching the model name (or architecture slug). If no template is found, `HFChatTemplate` is used as fallback.

### Mermaid Diagram: Natural Language Concepts to Code Entities

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Natural Language Concepts"
        MessagesArray["OpenAI-style Messages (list of dict)"]
        ModelIdentifier["Model Path / Family Name"]
        ChatPromptStr["Formatted Prompt String"]
    end

    subgraph "Code Entities (lmdeploy package)"
        CTConfig["ChatTemplateConfig (lmdeploy/model.py:35)"]
        MODELSReg["MODELS Registry (lmdeploy/model.py:14)"]
        BaseChat["BaseChatTemplate messages2prompt() (lmdeploy/model.py:162)"]
        HFTemplate["HFChatTemplate (lmdeploy/model.py:678)"]
        TokenizerWrap["HuggingFaceTokenizer (lmdeploy/tokenizer.py:39)"]
        ArchDetect["autoget_backend (lmdeploy/archs.py:10)"]
        TurboMindSupport["is_supported (lmdeploy/turbomind/supported_models.py)"]
    end

    MessagesArray --> CTConfig
    ModelIdentifier --> ArchDetect
    ArchDetect -->|selects backend| TurboMindSupport
    CTConfig -->|selects| MODELSReg
    MODELSReg -->|provides template| BaseChat
    MODELSReg -->|fallback| HFTemplate
    BaseChat -- formats --> ChatPromptStr
    HFTemplate -- formats via TokenizerWrap --> ChatPromptStr
```

**Sources:** [lmdeploy/model.py](), [lmdeploy/archs.py](), [lmdeploy/turbomind/supported_models.py](), [lmdeploy/tokenizer.py]()

# Technical Details and Examples

### Example: Using a ChatTemplateConfig to get a prompt

```python
from lmdeploy.model import ChatTemplateConfig, MODELS

config = ChatTemplateConfig(model_name='llama2', user='USER:', assistant='ASSISTANT:')
template = config.chat_template()
messages = [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Hello, how are you?'}]
prompt = template.messages2prompt(messages)
print(prompt)
```

This converts a message list into a formatted prompt string using the registered `llama2` template.

### Example: Fallback to HuggingFace tokenzier prompt application

If a model has no registered template, the fallback `HFChatTemplate` will apply the tokenizer's native template:

```python
from lmdeploy.model import ChatTemplateConfig

config = ChatTemplateConfig(model_name='hf', model_path='Qwen/Qwen3-8B')
template = config.chat_template()
messages = [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Hello!'}]
prompt = template.messages2prompt(messages)
print(prompt)  # Uses tokenizer.apply_chat_template()
```

---

# Summary

LMDeploy's chat template and tokenization system enables flexible and modular prompt formatting tailored for a wide variety of LLMs. Through the `ChatTemplateConfig` dataclass and `MODELS` registry, it supports both explicit templates for popular models and an automatic HuggingFace tokenizer-based fallback for newer or custom models. Together with architecture detection and backend selection, this system forms a robust bridge from general OpenAI-style chat messages to concrete prompt strings optimized for each model's inference engine.

This document details the technical implementation of model loading, conversion, and weight management in LMDeploy. It covers the architecture for both the TurboMind and PyTorch engines, focusing on how raw model weights are transformed into inference-ready formats, how tensor parallelism (TP) is applied, and the role of specialized weight loaders.

---

## Model Loading Architecture

LMDeploy supports loading models from HuggingFace, ModelScope, and pre-converted TurboMind formats. The system uses a registry-based approach to map model architectures to specific implementation classes. Model architecture identification is performed via the `get_model_arch` function [lmdeploy/archs.py:5](), and TurboMind-supported architectures are listed in the `SUPPORTED_ARCHS` constant [lmdeploy/turbomind/supported_models.py:14]().

### Architecture Detection and Registration

Models are registered centrally in registries such as `INPUT_MODELS` for TurboMind text models and `VISION_MODELS` for vision model components. These registries map string keys to model implementation classes.

```mermaid
%% Title: Model Registration and Loading Flow
graph TD
    subgraph "Registry Space"
        TM_REG["INPUT_MODELS (Registry)"]
        VLM_REG["VISION_MODELS (Registry)"]
    end

    subgraph "Code Entity Space"
        Llama["LlamaModel"]
        InternVL["InternVLModel"]
        InternVLVision["InternVLVisionModel"]
    end

    TM_REG -- "registers" --> Llama
    TM_REG -- "registers" --> InternVL
    VLM_REG -- "registers" --> InternVLVision

    HF_CFG["HuggingFace Config"] --> ArchDetect["get_model_arch()"]
    ArchDetect --> TM_REG
    TM_REG --> Instantiation["Model Class Instantiation"]
```

This design decouples architecture detection from implementation, allowing flexible extension to new models.

Sources: [lmdeploy/turbomind/models/base.py:12](), [lmdeploy/turbomind/supported_models.py:14](), [lmdeploy/vl/model/internvl.py:28]()

---

## TurboMind Conversion and Weight Format Resolution

The TurboMind engine relies on a set of `WeightFormat` abstractions that define how raw checkpoint tensors are interpreted, quantized, and formatted for efficient CUDA kernel execution.

### WeightFormat and Resolver

The abstract base class `WeightFormat` specifies the interface for loading and normalizing weights into TurboMind's preferred layout. Key format implementations include:

| Format Class      | Quantization        | Block Size / Layout              | Source                                  |
|-------------------|---------------------|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| `TrivialFormat`   | None (FP16/BF16)     | Raw tensor, possible transpose  | [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:177]() |
| `AWQFormat`       | AWQ INT4             | Blocked by `block_in` group size| [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:236]() |
| `GPTQFormat`      | GPTQ INT4            | Blocked by `block_in` group size| [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:284]() |
| `FP8Format`       | FP8 (E4M3/E5M2)      | 128x128 block                   | [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:447]() |

Utility functions like `pack_u4_row` pack two 4-bit values into a 32-bit int to ensure layout compatibility for INT4 quantization.

A `WeightFormatResolver` class queries available suffixes on checkpoint keys (e.g., `.qweight`, `.scales`, `.g_idx`) to dynamically select the appropriate weight format during conversion [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:522]().

### Conversion Logic

The conversion process involves the following steps:

1. **Dtype Resolution**

   The function `_resolve_dtype` selects between FP16 and BF16 precision based on the runtime environment and hardware capabilities, ensuring TurboMind runs with optimal numeric precision [lmdeploy/turbomind/converter.py:127-151]().

2. **Layout Normalization**

   Each `WeightFormat` subclass implements the `normalize()` method, generating a tensor layout compatible with TurboMind's CUDA kernels. This may include reordering, permutation, or quantizing the raw tensor [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:109]().

3. **Packing and Quantization**

   For 4-bit quantizations, weights are packed into 32-bit containers with `pack_u4_row`, which combines every pair of 4-bit values along the row dimension. This packing is essential for efficient GPU memory access patterns [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:63-74]().

Sources: [lmdeploy/turbomind/weight_format.py:24-121](), [lmdeploy/turbomind/converter.py:29-56]()

---

## PyTorch Engine Weight Loading

The PyTorch engine employs a flexible and scalable weight loading mechanism via `ModelWeightLoader`. This loader supports both sharded and monolithic checkpoints in either safetensors or PyTorch format.

### ModelWeightLoader Process

1. **Shard Discovery**

   `_get_shard_paths` locates all checkpoint shard files, using weight index files (`weights.json` or `weights.index.json`) to enumerate shards for sharded models [lmdeploy/pytorch/weight_loader/model_weight_loader.py:128-137]().

2. **Weights Iteration**

   Depending on the weight type, `_get_weights_iterator` opens each shard to yield (name, tensor) pairs lazily. This abstracts over safetensors or PyTorch `.pt` files [lmdeploy/pytorch/weight_loader/model_weight_loader.py:139-145]().

3. **Weight Key Renaming**

   Models may define a `rename_weight` method to map or rename checkpoint keys to the framework's internal naming convention. This is applied via the `_rename_weights_iterator` wrapper [lmdeploy/pytorch/weight_loader/model_weight_loader.py:155-160]().

4. **Loading Weights**

   The loader invokes the model’s `load_weights` function passing the iterator over weights. The model-specific loader applies weights to individual modules using the `load_weight` function, which either uses a custom loader or a fallback `default_weight_loader` to copy tensor data [lmdeploy/pytorch/weight_loader/model_weight_loader.py:162-190]().

```mermaid
%% Title: PyTorch Weight Loading and Linear Sharding
graph LR
    subgraph "Weight Loading"
        MWL["ModelWeightLoader"]
        ITER["Weights Iterator"]
        LW["load_weight()"]
    end

    subgraph "Linear Sharding (TP)"
        BCWL["build_colwise_linear"]
        BRWL["build_rowwise_linear"]
        BQKV["build_qkv_proj"]
    end

    MWL --> ITER
    ITER --> LW
    LW --> BCWL
    LW --> BRWL
    LW --> BQKV
```

Sources: [lmdeploy/pytorch/weight_loader/model_weight_loader.py:115-190](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/internvl.py:18-20]()

---

## Tensor Parallelism and Distributed Loading

LMDeploy implements Tensor Parallelism (TP) by sharding linear weights during the load phase and handling distributed communication accordingly.

### Linear Layer Sharding

Linear layers use two main sharding strategies based on their role in the model:

- **Column-wise Partitioning**

  The output feature dimension is split across tensor parallel ranks. Each rank loads a contiguous chunk of rows (out_features dimension). This is common for projections such as `gate_proj` and `up_proj`.

- **Row-wise Partitioning**

  The input feature dimension is split across ranks. Each rank receives a slice of columns (in_features dimension), performs its local matrix multiplication, and outputs are summed across ranks via an all-reduce operation. Used for projections like `o_proj` and `down_proj`.

These distribution sizes are computed with functions like `get_distribute_size` and `chunk_aligned`, which account for alignment requirements imposed by hardware and kernel implementations.

Tensor parallel group information and rank are retrieved via `get_tp_world_rank` and `get_dist_group` [lmdeploy/pytorch/nn/utils.py:10-36]().

### Vision-Language Model (VLM) Loading

For multimodal models such as InternVL, the vision encoder and language model are loaded and initialized separately:

- Vision weights (e.g., patch embedding, transformer blocks) are loaded with `load_weight`.

- The vision model tokenizes input images into patches, and maps those patches to tokens for the model's attention layers [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/internvl.py:137-160](), [lmdeploy/vl/model/internvl3_hf.py:56-86]().

This modular loading enables partial model updates and fused execution across modalities.

Sources: [lmdeploy/pytorch/nn/utils.py:10-36](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/internvl.py:12-20](), [lmdeploy/vl/model/internvl3_hf.py:56-86]()

---

## Weight Export and Initialization Optimization

LMDeploy provides utilities to optimize model loading speed and memory usage by bypassing standard PyTorch initialization overhead.

### LoadNoInit Context Manager

The `LoadNoInit` context manager temporarily replaces common PyTorch tensor initialization functions (`constant_`, `zeros_`, `ones_`, etc.) with no-op lambdas. This prevents redundant parameter initialization when weights will be overwritten immediately, saving memory and time during model instantiation [lmdeploy/lite/utils/load.py:9-45]().

Usage pattern:

```python
with LoadNoInit():
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...)
    model.config.use_cache = False
```

### Quantized Module Initialization

Quantized modules like `QLinear` and `QRMSNorm` are instantiated from their floating-point counterparts using class methods `from_float` which handle quantization of weights and proper initialization.

- `QLinear.from_float` performs per-channel 8-bit integer quantization of weights with corresponding float scales [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/q_modules.py:105-125]().

- Similarly, `QRMSNorm` encapsulates dynamic quantization of RMSNorm activations [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/q_modules.py:48-59]().

These methods enable seamless conversion from classic model weights to quantized modules optimized for memory and speed.

Sources: [lmdeploy/lite/utils/load.py:9-45](), [lmdeploy/pytorch/models/q_modules.py:48-125]()

---

# Summary

This section clarified LMDeploy's end-to-end model loading and conversion pipeline including:

- Automatic architecture registration and model instantiation.
- TurboMind-specific weight format abstractions and conversion logic for various quantized formats.
- Robust PyTorch engine weight loading with shard and key renaming support.
- Tensor parallelism-aware weight sharding for distributed execution.
- Utilities for fast model initialization bypassing default weight init.
- Quantized module construction to facilitate low-precision inference.

Together, these components provide a flexible and efficient system for preparing large language and multimodal models for deployment across diverse hardware setups.

```mermaid
    end

```

This document covers LMDeploy's quantization capabilities for reducing model memory usage and improving inference performance. LMDeploy supports multiple quantization techniques, including W4A16 AWQ, W8A8 SmoothQuant, GPTQ, KV INT4/8, and FP8, along with comprehensive calibration infrastructure for optimal results.

## Quantization Architecture Overview

LMDeploy's quantization system provides a unified interface for multiple algorithms while supporting various model architectures and deployment backends (TurboMind and PyTorch). It integrates quantization-aware calibration pipelines and modular quantization implementations to enable flexible compression and efficient inference.

### System Data Flow and Code Entities

The following diagram illustrates the bridge between Natural Language quantization concepts and the corresponding code entities across LMDeploy, facilitating mapping from user commands through calibration to quantization implementations.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Natural Language Space"
        UserCmd["CLI Command: lmdeploy lite auto_awq / smooth_quant / auto_gptq"]
        AlgoChoice["Algorithm: AWQ / SmoothQuant / GPTQ / FP8 / KV INT4/8"]
        CalibData["Calibration Dataset & Parameters"]
        ModelArch["Model Architecture: Llama, InternLM2/3, Qwen2/3, etc."]
    end

    subgraph "CLI Interface"
        LiteCLI["lmdeploy.cli.lite.SubCliLite"]
    end

    subgraph "Backend APIs"
        AutoAWQ["lmdeploy.lite.apis.auto_awq.auto_awq()"]
        SmoothQuant["lmdeploy.lite.apis.smooth_quant.smooth_quant()"]
        GPTQ["lmdeploy.lite.apis.gptq.auto_gptq()"]
        Calibrate["lmdeploy.lite.apis.calibrate.calibrate()"]
    end

    subgraph "Quantization Core"
        AWQCore["lmdeploy.lite.quantization.awq"]
        GPTQCore["lmdeploy.lite.apis.gptq"]
        SmoothCore["lmdeploy.pytorch.nn.linear.w8a8 / lmdeploy.pytorch.nn.linear.awq"]
        FP8Core["lmdeploy.pytorch.backends.cuda.blockedf8_modules / kernels"]
        KVCore["lmdeploy.pytorch.nn.linear.kv_cache_int4 / int8"]
    end

    subgraph "Calibration Infrastructure"
        CalibCtx["lmdeploy.lite.quantization.CalibrationContext"]
        Obs["lmdeploy.lite.quantization.ActivationObserver"]
        LayerMap["lmdeploy.lite.apis.calibrate.LAYER_TYPE_MAP"]
    end

    UserCmd --> LiteCLI
    LiteCLI --> AutoAWQ
    LiteCLI --> SmoothQuant
    LiteCLI --> GPTQ
    LiteCLI --> Calibrate

    AutoAWQ --> Calibrate
    SmoothQuant --> Calibrate
    GPTQ --> Calibrate

    Calibrate --> CalibCtx
    CalibCtx --> Obs
    AutoAWQ --> AWQCore
    SmoothQuant --> SmoothCore
    GPTQ --> GPTQCore
```
